docs.title: lipipy
docs.text:
Readable, verified-from-scratch implementations of machine learning, deep learning and modern research architectures.

Every algorithm is readable (the math is in the docstring), verified (tested for parity against scikit-learn or PyTorch) and explained (paired with a notebook).

pip install -e ".[dev]"

from lipipy.ml import LinearRegression

model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)

docs.title: Dependencies and from-scratch inventory
docs.text:
Status: researched 2026-11-11 against PyPI. Refresh the version tables with make deps-report before each release (see §7).

This document answers two questions for every part of lipipy:

  1. What do we depend on? Third-party packages by role: runtime, optional extras, reference libraries used only in tests, and tooling.
  2. What do we write ourselves? The from-scratch code each layer needs, and the order to build it in.

It complements ARCHITECTURE.md (§3 layers, §6 complexity) and SECURITY.md.

docs.title: 1. Dependency principles
docs.text:
1. One required runtime dependency: NumPy. pip install lipipy must stay small and import fast. Everything else is an optional extra or test-only.
  2. Extras unlock backends and domains, never core features. A feature that needs an extra imports it through lipipy.core.require(module, extra=...), which fails with an install hint.
  3. Reference libraries are for verification only. scikit-learn, SciPy, Qiskit, QuantLib and others are used in parity tests to check our implementations. lipipy never wraps them as its own implementation.
  4. Permissive licences only. Runtime and extras: MIT, BSD, Apache-2.0, ISC, PSF, NCSA, Zlib. MPL-2.0 is acceptable for development tools only. GPL/AGPL/SSPL or proprietary packages are not allowed in any extra.
  5. Lower bounds, no upper caps in pyproject.toml (a library must not cap its users' versions). Reproducibility comes from CI and lock files, not from pins in the package.
  6. No network or data-vendor packages as dependencies. Market-data downloaders, scrapers and LLM provider SDKs stay out of the package; examples may show them.

docs.title: 2. Python version support
docs.text:
Fact (PyPI, 2026-11) Requires NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, JAX 0.12, NetworkX 3.7 Python ≥ 3.12 PyTorch 2.15, scikit-learn 1.9, pandas 3.1, Qiskit Aer 0.18, PennyLane 0.45, cvxpy 1.9 Python ≥ 3.11

Decision: requires-python = ">=3.11" and CI on 3.11, 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14. Python 3.10 is dropped because most extras can no longer be installed on it. We follow the Scientific Python SPEC 0 direction (support Python versions for about three years) but move one step behind it, so users on 3.11 are not stranded. Revisit at each minor release; the next step is 3.12.

docs.title: 6. From-scratch inventory and build order
docs.text: What lipipy writes itself. Policy: numerics contains readable from-scratch implementations (verified against SciPy/NumPy). Domain algorithms may call NumPy's LAPACK-backed primitives (np.linalg.lstsq, svd, eigh) for speed and stability, and must say so in their docstring. Each item lists what it builds on.

docs.title: 6.1 Cross-cutting infrastructure (layer 0, core)
docs.text: Component Status Builds on Registry, Complexity, backends, random, errors, optional imports done numpy Estimator protocols (Estimator, Transformer, Classifier as typing.Protocol) next core.base Result dataclasses with .to_dict() (OptimizeResult, FitResult, …) next dataclasses Safe serialization: save/load via .npz with allow_pickle=False + JSON metadata planned numpy Synthetic dataset generators (regression, blobs, moons, time series, price paths) planned core.random Input-size guards from declared complexity (ResourceLimitError) planned registry

docs.title: 6.2 Build order (critical path)
docs.text:
core ─► numerics.special ─► numerics.stats ─► numerics.linalg ─► numerics.optimize ─► numerics.autodiff
            │                      │                 │                  │                    │
            │                      │                 │                  ├─► ml (logistic, SVM, …)
            │                      │                 ├─► quantum (statevector, gates)        └─► dl (teaching autograd)
            │                      └─────────────────┴─► finance (risk, portfolio, pricing)
            └─► numerics.fft / integrate / ode ─► finance (PDE pricing), research (SSM kernels)

docs.title: 6.3 Per-layer scratch code
docs.text:
numerics (layer 1) — the foundation every domain reuses

Order Module Contents Key complexity 1 special stable logsumexp, softmax, sigmoid, log1pexp; vectorized erf/erfc (NumPy has none) and normal cdf/ppf O(n) 2 stats Welford mean/variance (streaming), covariance, quantiles, distributions (pdf/cdf/sample) O(n d²) for covariance 3 linalg triangular solves, LU with pivoting, Cholesky, Householder QR, power/QR eigen iteration, CG, GMRES O(d³) dense, O(nnz·T) iterative 4 optimize Armijo/Wolfe line search, gradient descent, Newton, BFGS, L-BFGS, Nelder-Mead, projected gradient, simplex, QP per-iteration O(d) to O(d³) 5 autodiff forward mode (dual numbers), reverse-mode tape for scalars then tensors, gradient check ≈ 2–4× forward cost 6 fft radix-2 Cooley-Tukey, real FFT, FFT convolution O(n log n) 7 integrate, ode, sde Simpson, Gauss-Legendre, adaptive quadrature; RK4, RK45, implicit Euler; Euler-Maruyama O(T) steps 8 interpolate, sparse cubic splines; COO/CSR with matvec O(n); O(nnz)

ml (layer 2): metrics and preprocessing → linear models (logistic uses optimize.lbfgs) → kNN with chunked distances (memory O(n·chunk), not O(n²)) → trees (sorted-split search O(n d log n)) → ensembles → clustering (k-means++) → PCA via SVD → probabilistic models (EM, HMM).

ai (layer 2): problem/state protocols → BFS/DFS/UCS/A* with a binary heap (heapq) → CSP backtracking with AC-3 → DPLL/CDCL SAT → minimax/alpha-beta → MCTS.

quantum (layer 2)

Order Component Notes 1 states basis/product states, normalization checks, Bloch coordinates 2 gates unitary matrices; is_unitary check (‖U†U − I‖ < tol) 3 statevector apply a k-qubit gate by reshaping the state to (2,)*q and np.tensordot / einsum on the target axes: O(2^q · 2^k) time, no 2^q × 2^q matrix; max_qubits guard 4 measure probabilities, shots via rng.choice, Pauli-string expectations 5 Circuit fluent builder, parameters, depth/gate counts 6 algorithms QFT, Grover, phase estimation, Deutsch-Jozsa, teleportation 7 variational parameter shift, VQE and QAOA using numerics.optimize 8 density_matrix, noise, mps, stabilizer O(4^q); O(q χ²); polynomial

finance (layer 2)

Order Component Builds on Notes 1 returns, volatility, Sharpe/Sortino, drawdown stats pure functions over (T,) or (T, A) arrays 2 VaR / CVaR, covariance shrinkage (Ledoit-Wolf) stats, linalg 3 Black-Scholes and Greeks, implied volatility special.ndtr, optimize (Brent/Newton) 4 binomial trees, Monte Carlo (antithetic, control variates) core.random chunk over paths: memory O(chunk·T) 5 Markowitz, min-variance, risk parity, Black-Litterman linalg, optimize (QP) 6 vectorized backtester → event-driven backtester all of the above time-indexed data view prevents look-ahead; costs required

dl (layer 2): thin modules on PyTorch (layers, losses, optimizers written out explicitly) plus a teaching path on numerics.autodiff for a NumPy-only MLP.

rl (layer 3): Env protocol compatible with Gymnasium → tabular methods → bandits → DQN/PPO on dl.

research, interpret (layer 3) and agents (layer 4): build on the layers above; agents add the provider-neutral LLM protocol, tool schemas generated from the registry and type hints, and the MCP server.

docs.title: 7. Keeping this document current
docs.text:
• Dependabot opens weekly PRs for GitHub Actions and Python tooling.
  • Before each release: refresh the version tables from PyPI, run make security (pip-audit, bandit, secret scan, licence check) and update the Python support line.
  • Adding a dependency requires: the role (§3–5), licence check against §1, why a from-scratch implementation is not appropriate, and a line in this file.

docs.title: Linear Regression
docs.text:
Notebook: notebooks/ml/01_linear_regression.ipynb

Ordinary least squares linear regression.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
.. math:: \hat y = X w + b

We pick w and b to minimise the mean squared error

.. math:: L(w, b) = \frac{1}{n} \lVert y - Xw - b \rVert_2^2 .

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
"lstsq" (default) Closed form. Centring X and y removes the intercept, then we solve :math:\min_w \lVert X_c w - y_c \rVert^2 with an SVD-based least-squares routine. This is the numerically stable version of the normal equation :math:w = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y and also handles rank-deficient X. The intercept is recovered as :math:b = \bar y - \bar x^\top w.

"gd" Batch gradient descent, included for teaching. The gradients are

.. math::
    \nabla_w L = -\tfrac{2}{n} X^\top (y - \hat y), \qquad
    \nabla_b L = -\tfrac{2}{n} \textstyle\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i).

Features are standardised internally so a single learning rate works
across datasets, and the weights are mapped back to the original scale.

Reference: Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., section 3.2.

docs.title: LinearRegression
docs.text:
Bases: RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator

Ordinary least squares linear regression.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: fit_intercept : bool, default=True Whether to learn a bias term b. solver : {"lstsq", "gd"}, default="lstsq" "lstsq" solves in closed form; "gd" uses batch gradient descent. learning_rate : float, default=0.1 Step size for solver="gd". max_iter : int, default=10_000 Maximum number of iterations for solver="gd". tol : float, default=1e-10 solver="gd" stops when the loss improves by less than tol.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text: coef_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,) Learned weights w. intercept_ : float Learned bias b (0.0 when fit_intercept=False). n_iter_ : int Iterations run (1 for "lstsq"). loss_history_ : list of float Training MSE per iteration ("gd" only, empty otherwise).

docs.title: Complexity
docs.text: solver="lstsq": time O(n d^2 + d^3), extra space O(n d). solver="gd": time O(T n d) for T iterations, extra space O(n d).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
import numpy as np from lipipy.ml import LinearRegression X = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]]) y = 2 * X[:, 0] + 1 model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y) round(float(model.coef_[0]), 6), round(model.intercept_, 6) (2.0, 1.0)

Source code in src/lipipy/ml/linear/linear_regression.py 
@register(
    domain="ml",
    tasks=("regression",),
    complexity=Complexity(
        time="O(n d^2 + d^3)",
        space="O(n d)",
        notes="solver='gd' costs O(T n d) time; both keep one centred copy of X",
    ),
    references=(
        "Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., §3.2",
    ),
    status="stable",
)
class LinearRegression(RegressorMixin, BaseEstimator):
    """Ordinary least squares linear regression.

    Parameters
    ----------
    fit_intercept : bool, default=True
        Whether to learn a bias term ``b``.
    solver : {"lstsq", "gd"}, default="lstsq"
        ``"lstsq"`` solves in closed form; ``"gd"`` uses batch gradient descent.
    learning_rate : float, default=0.1
        Step size for ``solver="gd"``.
    max_iter : int, default=10_000
        Maximum number of iterations for ``solver="gd"``.
    tol : float, default=1e-10
        ``solver="gd"`` stops when the loss improves by less than ``tol``.

    Attributes
    ----------
    coef_ : ndarray of shape (n_features,)
        Learned weights ``w``.
    intercept_ : float
        Learned bias ``b`` (0.0 when ``fit_intercept=False``).
    n_iter_ : int
        Iterations run (1 for ``"lstsq"``).
    loss_history_ : list of float
        Training MSE per iteration (``"gd"`` only, empty otherwise).

    Complexity
    ----------
    ``solver="lstsq"``: time O(n d^2 + d^3), extra space O(n d).
    ``solver="gd"``: time O(T n d) for T iterations, extra space O(n d).

    Examples
    --------
    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from lipipy.ml import LinearRegression
    >>> X = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
    >>> y = 2 * X[:, 0] + 1
    >>> model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
    >>> round(float(model.coef_[0]), 6), round(model.intercept_, 6)
    (2.0, 1.0)
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        fit_intercept: bool = True,
        solver: str = "lstsq",
        learning_rate: float = 0.1,
        max_iter: int = 10_000,
        tol: float = 1e-10,
    ):
        self.fit_intercept = fit_intercept
        self.solver = solver
        self.learning_rate = learning_rate
        self.max_iter = max_iter
        self.tol = tol

    def fit(self, X, y) -> LinearRegression:
        X, y = check_X_y(X, y)
        if self.solver == "lstsq":
            self._fit_lstsq(X, y)
        elif self.solver == "gd":
            self._fit_gd(X, y)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown solver {self.solver!r}; use 'lstsq' or 'gd'.")
        return self

    def _fit_lstsq(self, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> None:
        if self.fit_intercept:
            x_mean, y_mean = X.mean(axis=0), y.mean()
            w, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X - x_mean, y - y_mean, rcond=None)
            self.intercept_ = float(y_mean - x_mean @ w)
        else:
            w, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
            self.intercept_ = 0.0
        self.coef_ = w
        self.n_iter_ = 1
        self.loss_history_ = []

    def _fit_gd(self, X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> None:
        n, d = X.shape
        # Standardise so one learning rate fits all datasets.
        mu = X.mean(axis=0) if self.fit_intercept else np.zeros(d)
        sigma = X.std(axis=0)
        sigma[sigma == 0] = 1.0
        Z = (X - mu) / sigma

        w, b = np.zeros(d), 0.0
        prev_loss = np.inf
        self.loss_history_ = []
        n_iter = 0
        for n_iter in range(1, self.max_iter + 1):  # noqa: B007 (used after loop)
            residual = y - (Z @ w + b)
            loss = float(np.mean(residual**2))
            self.loss_history_.append(loss)
            if prev_loss - loss < self.tol:
                break
            prev_loss = loss
            w += self.learning_rate * (2.0 / n) * (Z.T @ residual)
            if self.fit_intercept:
                b += self.learning_rate * (2.0 / n) * residual.sum()

        # Map back to the original feature scale.
        self.coef_ = w / sigma
        self.intercept_ = float(b - mu @ self.coef_) if self.fit_intercept else 0.0
        self.n_iter_ = n_iter

    def predict(self, X) -> np.ndarray:
        self._check_is_fitted("coef_")
        X = check_array(X)
        if X.shape[1] != self.coef_.shape[0]:
            raise ValueError(
                f"X has {X.shape[1]} features, but the model was fitted with {self.coef_.shape[0]}."
            )
        return X @ self.coef_ + self.intercept_
